beginner.headline: Countries fail to agree on major climate plan
beginner.brief: Countries at COP31 in Turkey failed to agree on a major plan to fight climate change. Countries disagreed about fossil fuels and money. Fossil fuels include coal, oil and gas. The talks were planned to end on Friday, but they continued until Sunday. The final plan did not mention fossil fuels. Some countries rejected the plan because it did not mention fossil fuels. Many poorer countries wanted clear promises of money from richer countries. They wanted help to deal with the effects of rising temperatures. The next climate talks are planned for November 2027 in Ethiopia.

intermediate.headline: COP31 Climate Deal Fails Over Fuels and Funding
intermediate.brief: Countries at COP31 in Turkey failed to reach a major new climate agreement because of deep divisions over fossil fuels and money. The negotiations continued from Friday into Sunday as countries searched for common ground. The EU and Pacific island nations found the final proposal unacceptable because it did not directly mention fossil fuels. Poorer countries also objected because richer nations made no clear financial commitments to help them adapt to rising temperatures. An earlier draft mentioned fossil fuels six times, but oil-producing nations found this unacceptable. At COP30 in Brazil last year, nations agreed to triple the financial support. However, this year's proposal included neither exact financial figures nor a starting amount for measuring that increase. This lack of detail raised concerns that richer nations would have too much freedom in how they met their promise. Although the main agreement failed, some progress was made on support for workers and communities moving towards clean energy. The climate process relies on consensus, which means countries must reach an agreement together. Following the failure, some people questioned whether this process could succeed in a politically divided world. The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on possible changes to the process.

advanced.headline: COP31 Deal Collapses Over Fossil Fuels and Finance
advanced.brief: Countries failed to secure a major new climate agreement at COP31 in Turkey after divisions over fossil fuels and finance emerged. The protracted discussions continued from their scheduled Friday finish into Sunday, making this the longest UN climate conference in history. Exhausted delegates received a fresh draft in the early hours of Sunday in an attempt to break the deadlock. The proposed agreement was unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it omitted any direct mention of fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming. Its only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas recalled the COP28 agreement to move away from fossil fuels in energy systems. Saudi delegate Mohammad Ayoub said Arab countries had participated in good faith, while arguing that their share of historical greenhouse gas emissions was small. Russia warned that moving away from fossil fuels too quickly would leave people unable to afford adequate energy. Not only did this year's deal omit concrete figures, but it also failed to specify the baseline against which the pledge would be measured. This lack of precision raised fears that richer nations would have excessive wriggle room in fulfilling the pledge. Chris Bowen, the Australian minister serving as COP31 president of negotiations, described delegates' red lines as irreconcilable. According to the UN, current government policies are likely to limit warming to about 2.8°C by 2100. Long-term warming is nevertheless likely to overshoot the Paris agreement's 1.5°C goal within the next few years. Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5°C, but this would require a major expansion of carbon dioxide removal technologies that do not yet operate at scale. Although the main agreement fell through, delegates made progress on a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy. The outcome prompted questions about whether a climate process that relies on consensus can succeed amid geopolitical divisions. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he would seek advice on procedural reform, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027 in Ethiopia.
